summary: Defines a MIB module for monitoring selectable performance metrics and statistics derived from network packets and sub-application level transactions. The metrics can be defined by reference to existing standards. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: A coach keeps score sheets to see how well a team plays. This memo gives network managers a standard score sheet for how well data transfers are going.

questions: how does tpm mib relate to rmon2
what statistics does the tpm mib report
subtitle: A standard SNMP MIB for measuring how well sub-application transactions perform on the network.

tldr.problem: Performance-monitoring agents measure things like response time and datagram loss, but with no standard way to report them, deployment stayed limited to specific customer needs.
tldr.mechanism: The TPM-MIB extends the RMON2-MIB and drills down below the APM-MIB. It reports metrics for sub-application transactions as raw statistical sums that a management application turns into averages and other figures.
tldr.outcome: Managers get a common framework to point at existing metric definitions and collect interval reports, with SNMPv3 security recommended because the data can be sensitive.

today: RFC 4150 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose and Place in the Framework
sections.content:
This memo defines a MIB module, a set of managed objects usually accessed through SNMP, defined in SMIv2. It continues the architecture of the RMON2-MIB (RFC 2021) and uses its Protocol Directory to report the layering involved in sub-application level transaction flows.

The lack of a standard way to report performance metrics had limited deployment to very specific customer needs. The RFC aims to be a general framework for collecting and reporting them. The objects are an interface between an RMON agent and a management application, not something for humans to manipulate directly.
sections.plainLanguage: Network devices can count how fast things go, but each one reported it differently. This memo gives them one shared form to fill in.

sections.title: Goals and the APM-MIB Drill-Down
sections.content:
The TPM-MIB complements the Application Performance Measurement MIB (RFC 3729), which gives aggregated data on the end user's view of application performance. A web page download, for instance, consists of DNS transactions, TCP connection establishment, an HTTP download of the base page and downloads of embedded objects. The TPM-MIB is meant to report on those individual sub-application transactions.

The stated objectives are a drill-down capability for trouble resolution, additional metrics and statistics, support for standards-based metrics, and, as an option, a table of raw per-transaction measurements. Metrics are described by reference to IETF, ITU or other documents through the tpmMetricDefTable, and tpmMetricDefGlobalID can point to a metric in the IPPM registry MIB (RFC 4148), or is set to 0.0 for none. No specific metric is mandatory, but implementations should at a minimum support a round-trip delay and a round-trip loss metric.

It does not measure the application's actual perceived performance; that is the APM-MIB's role.
sections.plainLanguage: Loading a web page is really many small steps. The end-user score says how long it all took, and this MIB shows how long each small step took.

sections.title: Structure of the MIB
sections.content:
The objects are arranged in four groups, which are the basic units of conformance: if an agent implements a group it must implement every object in it.

  • tpmCapabilitiesGroup shows the protocol and metric capabilities of the agent, mainly through tpmTransMetricDirTable and tpmMetricDefTable.
  • tpmAggregateReportsGroup holds aggregated statistics for configured report intervals, in tpmAggrReportCntrlTable and tpmAggrReportTable.
  • tpmCurrentReportsGroup covers transactions still in progress plus a history of completed ones, via tpmCurReportTable and tpmCurReportSize.
  • tpmExceptionReportsGroup links to notifications of transactions that exceed APM-MIB thresholds, in tpmExcpReportTable.
sections.plainLanguage: The score sheet has four parts: what the device can measure, summary scores, live scores for games in progress, and a list of times something went badly.

sections.title: How Statistics Are Reported
sections.content:
Storing every timestamp would take too much processing, memory and download time, and sampling packets would lose critical ones, so the agent processes the whole population of data. Instead of buckets, as in the APM-MIB, it keeps running sums and leaves the arithmetic to the management station, which avoids divisions, square roots and floating point in the agent.

Each statistic contains five unsigned integers: N (count of data points), S(X) (sum of values), S(X2) (sum of squared values), Xmax and Xmin, plus S(I*X), the sum of each value multiplied by its order. The mean is the sum divided by the count. Adjacent intervals combine by adding counts and sums and taking the maximum of the maxima and minimum of the minima, so two 30-second statistics can make a 60-second one. A datum a metric does not use defaults to 0.

From these the manager can derive number, frequency, maximum, minimum, range, arithmetic mean, root mean square, variance, standard deviation and the slope of a least-squares line.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of writing down every race time, the device keeps a running total and a count. Anyone can later divide to get the average, and two short tallies can be added into a longer one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The MIB describes passive monitoring and collects network layer addresses and statistics about conversations and application activity, which may be sensitive in some environments. Objects with read-write or read-create access, such as tpmTransMetricDirConfig, tpmAggrReportCntrlDataSource and tpmAggrReportCntrlAggrType, can affect network operation or expose client-level information if SET is allowed without protection. Readable tables such as tpmAggrReportTable and tpmCurReportTable also reveal traffic and current activity.

SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. Implementers are RECOMMENDED to consider SNMPv3 with its cryptographic authentication and privacy, and deploying earlier SNMP versions is NOT RECOMMENDED. Operators must configure access so only legitimate principals can GET or SET the objects.
sections.plainLanguage: Score sheets about who talked to whom could be private. So only the right people should be allowed to read or change them, and messages should be locked.
